ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: What is the smallest number of cells that need to be coloured in a $5 \times 5$ square grid so that every $1 \times 4$ or $4 \times 1$ rectangle in the grid has at least one coloured cell?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The attached images show an empty 5 by 5 square grid, matching the stated problem. Number the rows and columns from 1 to 5. In any fixed row, the two horizontal 1 by 4 rectangles are columns 1-4 and columns 2-5. Therefore each row must contain at least one coloured cell. Similarly, in any fixed column, the two vertical 4 by 1 rectangles are rows 1-4 and rows 2-5, so each column must contain at least one coloured cell. Hence at least 5 cells are needed. Suppose 5 cells were enough. Then, since there are 5 rows and 5 columns, there would have to be exactly one coloured cell in each row and exactly one in each column. If a row has only one coloured cell, it must lie in columns 2, 3, or 4, because it must hit both horizontal rectangles columns 1-4 and 2-5. Likewise, if a column has only one coloured cell, it must lie in rows 2, 3, or 4, because it must hit both vertical rectangles rows 1-4 and 2-5. But the coloured cell in row 1 is also the only coloured cell in its column, contradicting the fact that a singleton column cell must be in rows 2-4. Thus 5 cells are impossible. Now construct 6 cells: colour (1,3), (2,2), (3,1), (3,5), (4,4), and (5,3). Rows 1, 2, 4, and 5 each have a coloured cell in columns 2-4, so both horizontal 1 by 4 rectangles in those rows are hit. Row 3 has coloured cells in columns 1 and 5, so the rectangle columns 1-4 is hit by column 1 and the rectangle columns 2-5 is hit by column 5. For columns, columns 1, 2, 4, and 5 each have a coloured cell in rows 2-4, so both vertical 4 by 1 rectangles in those columns are hit. Column 3 has coloured cells in rows 1 and 5, so the rectangle rows 1-4 is hit by row 1 and the rectangle rows 2-5 is hit by row 5. Therefore 6 cells suffice, and since 5 are impossible, the minimum is 6.

raw_record.question_text: What is the smallest number of cells that need to be coloured in a $5 \times 5$ square grid so that every $1 \times 4$ or $4 \times 1$ rectangle in the grid has at least one coloured cell?

method.method_draft: Model the grid with rows and columns numbered 1 to 5. From the condition, observe that in each row the two horizontal 1x4 rectangles are columns 1-4 and 2-5, so every row must contain at least one coloured cell; similarly every column must contain at least one coloured cell. This gives a basic lower bound of 5 cells. Show 5 is impossible: with 5 cells, there would have to be exactly one coloured cell in each row and exactly one in each column. A row with only one coloured cell must have it in columns 2, 3, or 4 to hit both horizontal 1x4 rectangles. A column with only one coloured cell must have it in rows 2, 3, or 4 to hit both vertical 4x1 rectangles. But with one cell in every row, the cells in rows 1 and 5 would each be the only coloured cell in their columns, contradicting the requirement that singleton-column cells lie in rows 2-4. Hence at least 6 cells are needed. Then give a 6-cell construction, for example colour cells (1,3), (2,2), (3,1), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3). Check row by row and column by column that each has either a middle-position coloured cell or endpoint pair coverage, so every 1x4 or 4x1 rectangle is hit. Therefore the minimum is 6.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: This is a direct extremal/pigeonhole proof: establish a lower bound using row and column coverage, rule out the only possible 5-cell configuration, and match it with an explicit 6-cell construction.
planner_metadata.image_role: Use the image only as the blank 5x5 grid structure, identifying that there are 5 rows and 5 columns of cells with no pre-coloured cells or extra constraints.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question text to extract the requirement: choose the fewest coloured cells so that every horizontal 1x4 and vertical 4x1 rectangle in the 5x5 grid contains at least one coloured cell.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Use the hitting-set idea for length-4 intervals in a length-5 row/column: a single coloured cell hits both intervals only if it is in one of the middle three positions; otherwise endpoint-only coverage requires additional cells. Combine this with pigeonhole reasoning over rows and columns.
